parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man phones a storage company to rent a unit while his house is being renovated.
script: Good afternoon, Kestrel Self Storage, Dana speaking. How can I help you?
Oh, hello. I'm hoping to rent a storage unit for a few months. A friend of mine recommended you.
Lovely, I'm happy to help with that. I'll just take a few details first, if that's all right. Could I have your surname, please?
Thank you, Mr Hartnell. And a contact number?
07712 408 936. Got it. Now, what will you be storing with us?

Well, we're having the kitchen and the living room redone, so most of the furniture has to come out of the house. There's a sofa, a bed frame and a lot of boxes. Oh, and my son's drum kit, which I'm very keen to keep out of the house for a while.
Ha, I can imagine. Let me see. For that much, I'd normally suggest our 25 square foot unit. Actually, with a sofa and a bed frame, that might be a bit tight.
Yes, I thought it might be. I'd rather have more space than less.
Then I'd go for the 50 square foot unit. It's about the size of a small garage, so you'd have plenty of room to walk around things.
That sounds sensible. How much is that?
Normally it's 72 pounds a month, but we have an offer on for new customers at the moment. So it's 64 pounds 80 a month for the first six months.
Oh, that's good. Is there a minimum rental period?
Only four weeks. After that you can leave at a week's notice. So, when would you like to start?
The builders are due on the 10th of June, I think. No, wait, sorry, I've got that wrong. They're starting on the 12th of June, so I'd like the unit from that morning.
No problem, I'll put you down for the 12th of June. Is there anything else you want to know?
Where exactly are you? I'm not sure I know the area.

We're on the Ferry Road industrial estate, just behind the big furniture warehouse, so it's easy to find. There's plenty of parking right outside the units, and a trolley you can borrow if you need one.
That's useful. Is there anyone around to help with the heavy items?
The site manager is on duty during office hours and will happily lend a hand with a sofa, but he isn't here in the evenings, so it's worth bringing a friend.
I'll ask my brother. Do I pay by direct debit?
Yes, we take the first payment when you sign, and after that it comes out on the same day each month.
What about access? I might need to get things out in the evenings.
The office closes at 6, but the gate is open every day from 6 in the morning until 9.30 at night. It used to close at 8, but we extended it last year.
Excellent. And is the site secure?

Very. There are cameras, and a code for the gate. Each unit has a roller door, and you'll need your own padlock for it. We do sell them in the office, but they're quite expensive, so most people buy one beforehand.
Good idea. And what about insurance? Do I need my own?
Our standard policy covers your belongings up to 2000 pounds. If your furniture is worth more than that, you can upgrade to 5000 pounds for an extra 4 pounds a month.
I think I'd better do that. The sofa alone cost nearly that.

Right, I'll make a note of it. Now, when you come in to sign the agreement, please bring some photo ID, and proof of your address, such as a recent bill. A phone bill isn't accepted, I'm afraid. Our insurers insist on an electricity bill.
That's fine, I have one from last month. Anything else?
No, that's everything. We'll send a confirmation by text to the number you gave me. Thank you for calling, Mr Hartnell, and I hope the building work goes smoothly.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: The captain of a rowing club welcomes new members and shows them round the clubhouse.
script: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to Tidewater Rowing Club. My name's Graham, and I'm the club captain. I know a few of you are feeling a bit nervous, so let me say straight away that nobody here expects you to be an athlete. I'll tell you a little about the club, explain how your first few weeks will work, and then I'll take you on a quick tour of the clubhouse.

First, some history, because people are often surprised by it. Many assume the club was started by fishermen from the harbour, or perhaps by students, since there's a university just up the river. In fact it was founded in 1968 by two teachers from the local secondary school, who wanted to give their pupils a new sport to try. They borrowed one old boat and kept it in a shed, which is now our café. We've grown a good deal since then, and we now have about 200 members, from fourteen to eighty-one years old.

Now, the first thing you'll want to know is what happens in your first fortnight. Before you go out on the water, you'll take part in a safety session at the swimming pool in town. You may have heard that we ask for a swimming certificate. We used to, but we don't any more. What we do insist on is that everyone practises what to do if the boat tips over. It takes about forty minutes, it's good fun, and it's amazing how much more confident people are afterwards.

Beginners' sessions run on Saturday mornings, starting at 7.30. I know that sounds early, and some of you are already wincing. For a long time we ran them on Sunday afternoons, but the river is much calmer at the start of the day, and the wind tends to build later on. We did try weekday evenings for a while, but in winter it was simply too dark. So, Saturday mornings it is.

In those sessions you'll start in a wide, stable boat, with a coach in a motorboat alongside you. People always ask me what they'll find hardest. Most expect it to be the fitness, and some worry about balance. In practice, neither is the real problem. The hard part is rowing in time with the rest of the crew. If one person is a fraction out, the whole boat feels it. It takes weeks to get right, but when it works, it's a wonderful feeling.

A word about money. The annual membership fee is 180 pounds, and that includes the use of our gym. It doesn't include the club shirt, which is 25 pounds and entirely optional, and if you'd like a locker, that's a small extra charge. The boats are included, so you'll never pay to go out on the water.

You'll hear us talking about fundraising a lot this year. Two years ago we bought two new boats, so that's not the priority at the moment. Nor do we need to pay for coaching, as all our coaches are volunteers. What we urgently need is a new landing jetty, because the old one has become unsafe, and the council has told us we can't use it beyond next spring. So if you see a sponsored row or a cake sale, now you know why.

Right, let's walk round the building, so please follow me. We'll begin at the boat shed, where all the boats are kept. It's the most important area, so it's kept locked. You'll be given a code on your first day, and please don't share it with anyone who isn't a member. Next, upstairs, is the gym. I'm sorry to say it's closed at the moment, because the floor is being replaced, but it should reopen in October.

The changing rooms are along the corridor. They were repainted just last month, so they look much smarter than they did, though I can't promise they'll stay that way once the rowers get back from a wet morning on the river. And finally, the café. It's open to everyone, not just members, and it's where we hold our social events, such as the end-of-season dinner in November. The coffee is excellent, and the bacon rolls are even better.

That's about it from me. If you'd like to try a session, put your name on the list by the door, and bring a change of clothes and a towel. Does anyone have any questions before we go outside? No? Then let's make a start.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two psychology students discuss a study of memory and music and plan a class demonstration.
script: Hi, Raul. Thanks for meeting me. I've been reading the paper on music and memory for our seminar, and I'd like to go through it with you before we decide how to present it.
Sure. I've read it twice now. Remind me, why did you pick this one?
Honestly, because it went against what I believe. I always revise with music on, and the paper says it makes recall worse. That wasn't what I wanted to hear, so I wanted to look at it properly.
Fair enough. I thought you'd chosen it because Dr Ashworth recommended it.
She did mention it in a lecture, but I found it myself. Anyway, the participants. There were 60 of them, weren't there?

That's right, and they were all first-year psychology students who took part to earn course credit. They weren't paid, and there were no children or older people at all. So you could argue the sample isn't very typical.
Yes, that's a weakness. And the main finding? I know the headline, but I'd like the details.
Well, people remembered most in silence, and least when the music had words. Instrumental music was only slightly worse than silence, and the authors say that difference wasn't significant.
So the lyrics are the problem, not the music itself.
Exactly. What they didn't find, which a lot of people assume, is that instrumental music helps. It didn't.
Right. Now, the procedure. At first I thought the conditions were tested in different rooms, which would be a flaw.

I wondered that too, but they were all tested in the same laboratory. And the participants weren't told the aim until afterwards, so that's fine. What bothers me is the volume. The paper only says moderate, and it doesn't say how they measured it.
Oh, good point. If the songs with lyrics were louder, the effect might simply be about loudness.
I also wondered about the design. It would be stronger if every person had done all three conditions, wouldn't it?
They did, actually. Each person did silence, instrumental music and music with words, in a different order each time, so the comparison is fair. I liked that part of the design.
Oh, then I'll take that off my list of criticisms.
We should mention it in the presentation, though. It's the study's real strength.
Agreed, I'll put it on the slides.
Okay. So for the presentation, do we just summarise it, or do something more? I thought of running a survey about how students study.
Mr Patel said we could do a short demonstration with the class. A survey would only give us opinions, not actual memory scores, and I think a video would take too long to make.
A live demonstration it is, then. That's more fun anyway. Let's plan it now, and I'll write it down.
Fine. Who are our participants? The whole class would be too many.
Volunteers from our tutorial group, then. About twelve, I'd say.
Good. And the word lists? The original study used twenty words, but we only have a few minutes.
I was going to suggest thirty. But you're right, that's too many. Is 15 enough?
Yes, 15 is plenty. And for the music, should we use speakers?
Speakers would disturb the rest of the class. Headphones, I think.
Agreed. How long do they get to write down what they remember? Five minutes?
That's long. 3 minutes is enough, I think.
They'll write their answers on paper, and then we put the results into a spreadsheet so we can make a chart for the slides.
I'll do the spreadsheet. You do the word lists, and we'll ask Mr Patel to check the plan on Thursday.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer talks about mangrove forests: how they survive, why they matter and how they can be restored.
script: Good morning. Today I'd like to talk about mangrove forests, which are among the most productive and the most threatened ecosystems on the planet. Mangroves are not a single species. They are a group of more than seventy species of trees and shrubs which share one thing: they grow along tropical and subtropical coasts, in what's known as the intertidal zone, the strip of shore that is covered by sea water at high tide and exposed at low tide.

Living there is difficult. The soil is waterlogged, it contains very little oxygen, and it's salty. So mangroves have evolved some remarkable adaptations. Take the roots. Red mangroves, for example, have stilt roots, which arch out from the trunk like the legs of a spider and anchor the tree in soft mud. Other species send up roots like tiny snorkels, which take in air at low tide.

Then there's the problem of salt. Some mangroves block most of it at the roots. Others take it in, and then get rid of it through special glands in their leaves. If you look closely at a leaf of one of these species, you'll often see white crystals on the surface. You'll be pleased to hear that I don't recommend tasting them.

Now, why do mangroves matter? First, biodiversity. The tangled roots form a kind of nursery. Prawns and crabs shelter there, and so do young fish. Many of the fish caught commercially offshore, snapper for example, spend their first year among mangrove roots, so a fishery can depend on a forest that its fishermen never see. Add to this the birds, the monkeys and the insects, and you have a very rich habitat.

Second, carbon. Mangrove soils are waterlogged, so dead leaves and roots decay very slowly, and the carbon stays locked up in the mud for centuries. Per hectare, mangroves can store up to 4 times more carbon than a typical tropical rainforest. You'll sometimes see claims of ten times as much, but that figure applies only to the very richest sites, so 4 is the safer number to quote.

Third, protection. A dense belt of mangroves slows down waves. Studies carried out after cyclones found that a hundred metres of forest can reduce wave energy by up to 70 percent. Some publications say 90, but that figure comes from unusually wide forests. Whichever number you use, villages behind mangroves have generally suffered far less damage than villages without them.

Unfortunately, we have lost a great deal. Since 1980, about 35 percent of the world's mangroves have disappeared. Earlier estimates suggested that as much as half had gone, but better satellite mapping has brought that figure down. The rate of loss has slowed recently, which is encouraging, though it is still alarming.

What has caused it? People often think of palm oil plantations, or of ports and tourist resorts, and these certainly matter in some places. But the biggest single cause worldwide has been the clearing of mangroves to make way for shrimp farms. The ponds are often abandoned after only a few years, because the soil becomes too polluted, and by then the forest has gone.

So what can be done? Planting trees is the obvious answer, and donors love a photograph of a child holding a seedling. But many planting programmes fail. In some surveys more than half of the seedlings died, usually because they were planted in the wrong place, too low on the shore, where they simply drowned. In fact, the most successful projects hardly plant anything. They concentrate on restoring the natural tidal flow, and the seedlings then arrive by themselves on the water.

And finally, the projects that last are the ones in which local people have a reason to protect the forest. Where local fishermen are paid to monitor it, and are allowed to harvest crabs from it, survival rates have been much higher than where the plan was drawn up by officials far away, or where it depended on income from visiting tourists.
I'll stop there, and next week we'll look at the coral reefs that so often sit alongside mangroves. Please read the two articles on the reading list before then.

passages.title: Measuring the Year
paras: A  Almost every human society has needed some way of counting the days ahead. Farmers had to know when to sow, priests when to hold festivals, and tax collectors when payments fell due. The difficulty is that nature offers three units of time that do not fit together neatly: the day, the month, measured from one new moon to the next, and the year, the time the Earth takes to travel once around the Sun. A lunar month lasts about 29.5 days, and a year contains about 12.37 of them. A solar year is roughly 365.24 days. Every calendar in history is, in effect, a compromise between these awkward numbers, and the story of the calendar is largely the story of people trying to make that compromise work.

B  The earliest calendars were lunar, for the simple reason that the phases of the Moon are easy to see. Several Mesopotamian cities counted twelve lunar months, which gives a year of about 354 days, eleven days short of the seasons. Left alone, such a calendar slides backwards through the year, so that a harvest festival may drift from autumn into summer. Babylonian officials dealt with the problem by adding an extra month whenever the barley crop seemed to be running late. For centuries this practice, known as intercalation, was decided by royal decree rather than by any rule, and it was open to abuse: a ruler who wished to prolong his time in office, or to delay the collection of taxes, could simply order another month.

C  Egypt took a different course. Because the Nile flooded at a predictable time each year, shortly after the star Sirius first appeared in the sky before sunrise, the Egyptians were able to count the days between one flood and the next and found that they numbered about 365. Their civil calendar therefore consisted of twelve months of 30 days, followed by five extra days at the end of the year. It was simple, and administrators loved it, but it had a fatal flaw. The true year is about a quarter of a day longer, so the calendar lost one day every four years and, over a cycle of 1,460 years, travelled right around the seasons.

D  The Romans inherited something of a muddle. Their early calendar was a short one, and months were later added to fill the winter. An extra month was inserted from time to time by the priests known as pontiffs, who had a habit of lengthening or shortening years for political reasons. By the first century BC the calendar was months out of step with the seasons. In 46 BC Julius Caesar, advised by an Alexandrian astronomer named Sosigenes, imposed a thorough reform. He abolished the extra month, fixed the year at 365 days and added a leap day every fourth year, giving an average of 365.25 days. To bring the calendar back into line with the seasons, the year 46 BC was stretched to 445 days, which later Romans called the year of confusion.

E  The Julian calendar was a remarkable piece of engineering, and it lasted for more than sixteen centuries. But the solar year is not quite 365.25 days; it is about eleven minutes shorter. This is trivial in any single year, yet it accumulates at the rate of roughly one day every 128 years. By the sixteenth century the error had reached ten days, and the spring equinox was falling around 11 March instead of 21 March. This mattered to the Church, because the date of Easter depends on the spring equinox, and the festival was drifting steadily later into the spring. Churchmen had worried about the problem for generations.

F  The remedy was announced in 1582 by Pope Gregory XIII, on the advice of a commission of astronomers and mathematicians. Ten days were simply dropped: Thursday 4 October was followed by Friday 15 October. To stop the error building up again, a new rule was added. Century years would be leap years only if they were divisible by 400, so that 1900 was not a leap year in the new calendar, while 2000 was. This makes the average year 365.2425 days, so close to the true value that the calendar will take about 3,000 years to gain a single day.

G  Adoption of the new system was slow, and it was driven as much by politics as by science. Catholic countries such as Spain, Portugal and several Italian states changed at once, but many Protestant and Orthodox lands regarded the reform as a papal plot and refused. Britain and its colonies did not change until 1752, by which time eleven days had to be removed, and popular memory has it that crowds took to the streets demanding their missing days. Russia waited until 1918, and Greece until 1923. Even now, the Gregorian calendar is not the only one in use. The Islamic calendar is purely lunar, with a year of about 354 days, so that the month of Ramadan travels through every season in turn, and the Hebrew calendar adds a leap month seven times in every nineteen years to keep its festivals in step with the Sun.

passages.title: The Invisible Map
paras: A  Each summer, on beaches along the coast of eastern Florida, thousands of loggerhead turtle hatchlings dig their way out of the sand at night and scramble towards the surf. Within days they are swimming far from land, and for several years they will not come near a coast again. Instead they circle the North Atlantic, carried by a great clockwise system of currents known as a gyre, which stretches for thousands of kilometres. Many years later, the females that survive will return to lay their own eggs on the very stretch of coast where they were born. How can an animal with a brain no bigger than a walnut steer across an empty ocean and then find one particular beach? The question has occupied biologists for more than half a century.

B  Early theories looked to familiar clues. Perhaps the hatchlings followed the smell of the water, or the position of the Sun and stars. These ideas have difficulties. Hatchlings in the open ocean are surrounded by water that looks and smells much the same in every direction, and the sky is often hidden by cloud. Currents will carry them along, but they cannot be relied upon to keep the animals in the warm waters of the gyre; a young turtle swept into cold water at the edge could die. What the turtles needed, researchers reasoned, was a cue that works day and night, in all weathers. The Earth's magnetic field is one such cue. Because it is generated deep in the planet's core, it varies in a regular way across the surface: the angle at which its lines dip towards the ground changes steadily from the equator to the poles, and its strength changes too. Together, these two properties give almost every place in the ocean its own magnetic signature.

C  To test whether turtles can use such a signature, a team led by the biologist Ilse Brandvold built an unusual experimental tank. Newly hatched loggerheads were fitted with a lightweight tether attached to a rotating swivel, so that they could swim in any direction while a computer recorded their heading. Around the tank stood a framework of electrical coils, which allowed the team to reproduce the magnetic field found at different places in the ocean. The results were striking. When the field of a location near the northern edge of the gyre was created, the hatchlings turned to swim southwards, away from the cold. When the field of a location near its southern edge was used, they swam in a direction that would carry them back towards the middle of the gyre.

D  These findings suggested that the turtles are not merely using a compass, which would tell them where north lies. They seemed to possess something closer to a map, which tells them where they are as well. This is a remarkable conclusion, because the hatchlings used in the experiment had never swum in the open sea. They had hatched in a laboratory and spent their lives in tanks. Whatever they were doing, they were doing it without any previous experience of the places whose magnetic fields were being copied. The ability, in other words, appears to be inherited rather than learnt, and to be present from the first day of life.

E  The adults raise a different question: how do they find their way back to the beaches of their birth? One idea is that hatchlings learn the magnetic signature of their home coast as they leave it, and that the females recognise it again decades later. The theory gained support from an unexpected quarter. The magnetic field of the Earth drifts slowly over time, so that the signature of any particular place gradually changes. A survey of nest counts at Marlow Bay over twenty years found that the females' favourite nesting sites moved along the coast in step with these changes. The magnetic map is not perfectly precise, however. It can bring a turtle to within a few tens of kilometres of its target, but the final approach seems to depend on other cues, such as the chemistry of the coastal water.

F  How the turtles detect the field is still unknown. There are two main explanations. One proposes that their bodies contain tiny crystals of magnetite, a magnetic mineral, which behave like the needle of a compass and send signals to the nervous system. The other suggests that the field alters chemical reactions in light-sensitive molecules in the eye, so that the animal might in some sense see the field. Evidence for each exists, and some biologists believe that both mechanisms may be at work. Researchers have not yet settled the matter, partly because the experiments needed are extremely difficult to carry out on animals that spend most of their lives in the open ocean.

G  The discovery has practical implications. Turtles may be sensitive to disturbances of the field, and cables carrying electricity create their own fields, the effects of which on turtles have yet to be measured. Bright coastal lighting is already known to confuse hatchlings. There is a further concern about nests moved to protected hatcheries: if the hatchlings leave from a different place, they may imprint on the wrong signature. Similar abilities have been found in other animals, including salmon, spiny lobsters and many birds, and a better understanding of one species may help to protect others. For the loggerhead itself, the lesson is that its ancient and invisible map deserves to be taken seriously.

passages.title: The Case for the Zoo
paras: A  Few institutions divide opinion as sharply as the zoo. For its defenders it is an ark, a place where endangered species are bred and the public learns to care about them; for its critics it is a prison with a gift shop. Collections of wild animals are very old, from the menageries of ancient rulers to the Victorian gardens that first opened their gates to paying visitors, and the modern zoo has worked hard to distance itself from that history. Hundreds of millions of people visit zoos every year, and almost every zoo now presents itself as a centre for conservation, research and education. The question is whether those claims survive close examination. I shall argue that some of them do, but that fewer do than the zoo industry would like us to believe.

B  Take conservation first, since the modern zoo's moral case rests chiefly upon it. The successes are real and should not be dismissed. A few species, among them the Arabian oryx and the golden lion tamarin, were pulled back from the edge of extinction by captive breeding and returned to the wild. Yet these triumphs are a small part of the whole. The number of species successfully reintroduced is only a few dozen, while the number held in zoos runs to many thousands. Moreover, the animals that fill the enclosures are rarely the ones most in need. Elephants, giraffes and penguins are chosen because they draw crowds, not because they are close to extinction, while the true emergencies, among them obscure amphibians and freshwater fish, are largely absent, because nobody will pay to look at them.

C  The educational claim is weaker still. Zoo operators point to the millions of schoolchildren who pass through their gates, and it is pleasant to imagine each one leaving with a lifelong passion for wildlife. But studies that have observed visitors tell a more sober story. Most people spend a minute or two at each enclosure, often less, and surveys of attitudes taken before and after a visit have found little evidence of lasting change. I do not claim that a television documentary could replace the experience of standing a few metres from a living tiger; the sense of scale and presence is something no screen can give. But it is one thing to say that zoos provide a memorable day out and quite another to say that they make us wiser or kinder towards nature.

D  Then there is the welfare of the animals themselves, which is where my doubts are strongest. Species that range over vast areas in the wild, such as elephants, polar bears and big cats, seem to cope worst with captivity. Observers regularly record repetitive behaviour in such animals, notably swaying and pacing, which many scientists regard as a sign of distress. Zoos reply, fairly, that enclosures have improved out of all recognition, with larger spaces, natural surfaces and puzzle feeders to keep minds occupied. I welcome these changes. But an elephant that might walk thirty kilometres in a day cannot be given that freedom by even the most generous paddock, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise.

E  The strongest argument for zoos, in my view, is also the most modest. Defenders point out that the wild habitats of many species are shrinking so fast that a captive population is the last available insurance policy against extinction. I find this persuasive, up to a point. Insurance is only worth having, however, if there is somewhere to return the animals to, and that depends on protecting land rather than housing animals. The sums involved are revealing. The cost of keeping a single elephant in a good zoo for its lifetime might pay for rangers to guard a large area of forest for many years, and that forest would shelter thousands of species rather than one. Money spent on captive animals, in other words, is not always money well spent on conservation.

F  There is also an uncomfortable matter of money. Most zoos depend heavily on ticket sales, and ticket sales depend on charismatic animals. This creates a permanent tension between what the public wants to see and what conservation needs. A zoo that devoted its space to rare frogs would soon be bankrupt; one that keeps a polar bear will be full all summer. As long as zoos must please their paying visitors first, I suspect that conservation will always be the junior partner in the arrangement, however sincere the people who run them may be.

G  None of this leads me to call for the abolition of zoos. It leads me to ask a different question: not whether zoos are justified, but which zoos are. Those that can show that they breed endangered species for release, that spend a real share of their income on protecting habitat, and that keep animals in conditions where they can thrive deserve to continue. A zoo that cannot pass these tests, or that holds species which cannot thrive in captivity, should stop keeping them. The result would be fewer zoos with fewer species, and many visitors would be disappointed. I would argue that a smaller number of better institutions is a price worth paying. Whether the public, and the industry, will accept that is another matter.
